entities.summary:
Founded around 20 CE by Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, Tiberias was named in honor of the Roman Emperor Tiberius Caesar Augustus. Strategically situated on the southwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee (Kinneret), it swiftly became the capital of the Tetrarchy of Galilee and Perea, serving as a vital administrative and cultural hub in the Roman province of Judea. Its significance deepened profoundly in the wake of the Bar Kokhba revolt (132-136 CE), when it emerged as the preeminent center of Jewish scholarship and religious authority, hosting the Sanhedrin and becoming the primary seat for the development of Rabbinic Judaism.

Following the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE and the subsequent suppression of Jewish revolts, Tiberias absorbed a substantial influx of Jewish refugees and scholars, transforming it into a spiritual and intellectual beacon. It was here, between the 2nd and 5th centuries CE, that the Jerusalem Talmud (Talmud Yerushalmi) was compiled and redacted, a monumental work codifying Jewish law, ethics, and lore. The city's academies also developed the Tiberian vocalization system (Niqqud) for Hebrew, a critical innovation for preserving the accurate pronunciation and meaning of the Masoretic Text of the Hebrew Bible, influencing Jewish liturgy and scholarship globally.

Tiberias's intellectual legacy endured for centuries, profoundly shaping Jewish religious identity and practice. It remained a significant Jewish center through the Byzantine, early Islamic, Crusader, and Ottoman periods, though its political prominence waned. Its historical role as a sanctuary for Jewish learning after the loss of Jerusalem cemented its status as one of Judaism's Four Holy Cities, a designation that continues to draw pilgrims and scholars. The city's intellectual output, particularly the Jerusalem Talmud and the Tiberian vocalization, provided foundational texts and methodologies that underpin Jewish life and scholarship to this day.
